explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Matthew says Jesus went through all the towns and villages, "…teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness." Every disease and every sickness. I once fixed one crooked cookie and bragged about it for a week.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jesus went through all the towns and villages, "…teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness." So healing was part of the trip, right alongside the teaching and preaching. Every disease and every sickness, no town skipped.
That's it, baker. Matthew says Jesus was moved with compassion "…because they were harassed and helpless…" He saw what the crowds were carrying, and it moved Him.

explanations.answer: They are tired from following Him
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since crowds do get tired. But the text gives a different reason: "…because they were harassed and helpless…" (Matthew 9:36). Nothing there about tired feet or following Him. I think I'd be tired too, but I'd just be hungry for cookies.

explanations.answer: They have walked far from home
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd pick it, friend. But Matthew never says the crowds walked far from home. The reason it gives is that "…they were harassed and helpless…" (Matthew 9:36). That's what moved Him.

Right on, baker. The text says they were harassed and helpless, "…like sheep without a shepherd." Sheep with no one to lead them don't have much of a plan. I can relate, because I spent years stuck at the back of a junk drawer with no plan at all.
Ooh, that one sounds poetic, friend. But it's not the picture Matthew uses. He says the crowds were harassed and helpless, "…like sheep without a shepherd." No boats in this verse, just sheep.

Close to the farm, but not the picture, baker. The text says they were "…like sheep without a shepherd." The helplessness is about sheep with no one looking after them, not a field with no fence. A harvest does show up in the very next verse, though.

Careful there, friend. Jesus says, "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few." Plentiful harvest, few workers. That's a lot of work and not many hands. I know that feeling, because I've got a whole bakery and one mustache.
You got it, baker. Jesus says, "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few." So the harvest is big, and the workers are the part that's short. Lots to gather and not enough hands to do it.
That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest." Ask. Simple as that. The harvest belongs to the Lord, so the asking goes to Him.
Thanking is good, friend, and I do it every day. But that's not the word here. Jesus says, "Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest." The word is ask.

Praise is a fine thing to do, baker. But Jesus uses a different word in this verse: "Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest." He tells them to ask, because the workers are few.

Yes, baker. Matthew says Jesus "…gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness." The authority came from Him. Twelve disciples got handed something big.

Whoa, friend, that one sounds dramatic. But it's not in this passage. Matthew says Jesus "…gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness." No fire here, just that authority.

That's a big one, baker, but it's not what Jesus hands out here. Matthew says He "…gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness." Nothing about wind or sea in this passage.

Yes, friend. The text says "James son of Zebedee, and his brother John…" Two names, one pair of brothers, right next to each other on the list. Just like Peter and his brother Andrew right before them.

Not this time, baker. Matthew writes "James son of Zebedee, and his brother John…" So they are brothers. And the pair right before them, Simon called Peter and "…his brother Andrew…" are brothers too.
That's the one, baker. The list says "…Matthew the tax collector…" Name and job in one breath, like a name tag at a work event. No small talk needed.
Nice try, friend, but the list doesn't call Matthew that. It says "…Matthew the tax collector…" The list does name two sets of brothers, though: Peter and Andrew, and James and John.
Tentmaker, huh? I'd pay good money to see that, friend, but no. The list says "…Matthew the tax collector…" That's the job the text gives him.
Yes, baker. The list ends with "…Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus." That's a heavy way to end a list. I think it's a sad line, and the text doesn't say more here.
I see why you'd go there, friend, but that's not what this verse says about Judas. It says "…Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus." Betrayed is the word. It's a heavy ending to the list.
Not quite, baker. Matthew's last line on the list says "…Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus." Betrayed, not doubted. It's a heavy line, and the text leaves it right there.
